messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The night the aneurysm ruptured, Marcus had been sitting at his desk in the den, reviewing a budget proposal for the upcoming school year. He remembered the sudden, catastrophic pressure behind his eyes, the way his vision dissolved into a white noise of static, and the terrifying sensation of his own body becoming a trap he could not escape. He had been alone. His wife, Lena, had died three years earlier from ovarian cancer, and in that moment, as he lay on the floor unable to move his left side, he was certain he was following her. The emergency surgery saved his life, but it did not save the man he had been.

Now, fifteen months later, Marcus could not deliberately recall the details of that night. When he tried, the memory slipped away like water through his fingers, leaving only a frustrating blank. Yet the emotional weight of it would hit him without warning—a wave of pure, animal terror that surged through him in the middle of a staff meeting or while he was standing in the grocery store, with no image attached, only the feeling of his heart trying to escape his chest. Worse still were the bodily reenactments: a sudden stiffness in his left arm, a feeling that his head was being tilted back, and he would be back on that cold floor, paralyzed and waiting to die.

The world had become a landscape of traps. A whiff of hand sanitizer in the hallway at school could send him reeling, the antiseptic smell instantly conjuring the ICU. The sharp, sweet scent of alcohol from a parent’s breath at a conference made his stomach clench, a visceral reminder of the night he had been told he might not wake up. He began to dread his own annual physical, the cold stethoscope and the probing questions feeling like a prelude to another catastrophe. These triggers did not just disturb him; they confirmed a terrible new truth. He had come to believe that his own body was fundamentally unreliable, a ticking bomb he could no longer trust. The person he saw in the mirror—this hypervigilant, trembling man who flinched at a cough—was unrecognizable to him. He was certain he could not rely on himself to handle even a minor medical appointment, let alone another crisis.

In response, Marcus built a fortress of avoidance. He cut off all contact with his closest friends, cancelling dinners and ignoring calls, because every conversation felt like a minefield where someone might ask how he was doing. Before any interaction, whether with a teacher or a district superintendent, he would rehearse what he was going to say, running the script over and over in his head until it felt safe. He isolated himself completely, spending his evenings alone in his house, the silence a relief from the terror of unexpected questions. He refused to enter a hospital for any reason, even to visit a sick colleague, and he cancelled his annual physical three times. These strategies offered him a brittle sense of control, but they deepened his belief that he was a broken man. The more he isolated, the more he felt like a stranger to himself, and the more he rehearsed, the more he confirmed that he could not trust his own spontaneous responses.

The isolation also starved him of the very social support that might have helped his memory settle. Without anyone to talk to about what happened, the fragmented, terrifying intrusions grew only more powerful. Each sudden, image-less wave of panic or bodily reenactment further cemented his sense of being fundamentally damaged, a man who had lost his own autobiography. This, in turn, made him even more vigilant, scanning every room for the smell of antiseptic, every conversation for a medical reference. The cycle tightened until his world had shrunk to the size of his house, his job, and a narrow, rehearsed path between them.

What finally brought Marcus to a therapist’s office was not his own suffering, but a practical failure. During a fire drill at school, a first-grader had scraped her knee. The sight of the blood, the sudden proximity of a medical moment, sent Marcus into a full dissociative episode in front of the entire student body. He had frozen, unable to speak, his left arm stiffening as he felt himself back on that floor. The school board insisted he take a leave of absence. Sitting in the waiting room, he was terrified—not of the therapy itself, but of what it might unearth. He was most afraid that if he tried to remember that night deliberately, the memory would finally surface, and it would destroy whatever was left of him.
